result.summary: Leuconoë tells how the Sun exposed Venus and Mars to Vulcan, who trapped them in a net before the gods. In revenge Venus makes the Sun fall in love with Leucothoë, and he tricks his way into her chamber by disguising himself as her mother.

scenes.title: Leuconoë begins the Sun's tale
scenes.summary: After a pause, Leuconoë starts to tell of the Sun's loves, beginning with his sight of Venus and Mars.

scenes.title: Vulcan's net traps Venus and Mars
scenes.summary: The Sun tells Vulcan of the adultery. Vulcan forges a fine net and traps the lovers, then shows them to the laughing gods. Venus resolves to punish the Sun.
scenes.stakes: Venus and Mars face public disgrace; Vulcan's marriage bed has been wronged.

scenes.title: The Sun burns with new love
scenes.summary: The narrator addresses the Sun, whose passion for Leucothoë disrupts the hours and his light. Leucothoë's parentage is given.
scenes.stakes: The Sun neglects his duty to the world, driven by Venus's revenge.

scenes.title: The Sun disguised as Eurynome
scenes.summary: While his horses graze, the Sun enters Leucothoë's chamber as her mother, sends the maids away, reveals himself, and she yields.
scenes.stakes: Leucothoë's honour and safety before an overwhelming god.

alias_notes.explanation: Venus was linked with the island of Cythera.
Vulcan was associated with the island of Lemnos.
Patronymic; the Sun is a Titan descendant.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable statement of the Sun's all-seeing role, which causes his tale-bearing.
The gods' laughter at the trapped lovers is a famous comic moment.

analysis.text: Love as vengeance: the Sun's betrayal of Venus's secret is repaid by passion, a pattern of gods punished through desire.
The story is told by the Minyeides, who refuse Bacchus's rites and tell tales instead, showing Ovid's nested storytelling.

legacy.text: The tale of Mars and Venus caught in Vulcan's net, also in the Odyssey, was a favourite subject of Renaissance painters such as Tintoretto.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's version of the Sun's love for Leucothoë leads on to Clytie's jealousy and her transformation into a heliotropic flower.

language_notes.text: "Intrigue" here means a secret love affair; "discovers" means reveals or informs, not finds out.
"The husband, the son of Juno" is Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), the smith god, husband of Venus.
"Files out" means shapes by filing metal; the chains are so fine that the eye cannot see them.
"The Lemnian God" is Vulcan, associated with the island of Lemnos, where he was worshipped and where he landed when thrown from heaven.
"Could fain wish" means would gladly wish: some gods would gladly accept such disgrace to share Mars's pleasure.
"Cytherean" refers to Venus, linked with the island of Cythera, a centre of her worship.
Son of Hyperion: the Sun, whose father was the Titan Hyperion. The name is used here as a patronymic for the Sun god.
Refers to a solar eclipse, caused when the moon passes between the earth and the sun. The poet says the Sun's paleness has a different cause.
Clymene, Rhodos, Circe's mother and Clytie are earlier loves of the Sun. Clytie's jealous love for him is told later in this book.
Perfume-bearing nation: the Arabians, famed in antiquity for incense and spices.
Ambrosia: the food of the gods, said here to feed the Sun's horses instead of grass.
Distaff and spindle are tools for spinning thread; the distaff holds the wool or flax, and the spindle twists it.
Coursers: swift horses, here the horses that draw the Sun's chariot.

context_notes.text: As the Sun, he travels across the sky and sees everything below, which is why he can expose the lovers.
Venus's revenge leads to the Sun's tragic love for Leucothoë, the story that follows.
Orchamus is a Persian king. Achæmenian refers to Persia, named after the Achæmenid dynasty, and Belus is a legendary ancestor-king of the East.
The Sun sees everything, so he claims to be the universe's eye. This also hints that he knows the secret doings of gods and mortals.

literary_notes.text: "This God is the first…" is repeated for emphasis, and the second clause turns the particular event into a general truth about the Sun.
Comparing the net to threads and cobwebs exaggerates its delicacy to show Vulcan's extraordinary skill.
The gods' wish to share the disgrace undercuts their laughter; the humour mocks divine morals.
Venus repays the Sun in kind: he exposed her love, so she torments him with love.
The narrator breaks off to speak directly to the Sun, mocking his powerlessness against love and drawing the reader into the scene.
The Sun, who burns all lands, is now burnt by love's flame. The god who sees everything stares at only one girl.
The Sun's mental turmoil dims the sky and frightens mortals, so nature mirrors the god's emotions.
The comparison of mother and daughter exaggerates Leucothoë's beauty, which explains why the Sun is so taken with her.
Her fear makes her more attractive to the Sun. This shows the god's desire and the girl's helplessness, a pattern common in Ovid's love stories.
